During the height of the trade war between Trump and China, tariffs were announced almost weekly, prompting companies such as Logitech to sharply raise prices on their products in the United States.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled that those tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. Yet so far no company has been seen passing the refunds on to consumers, and a class action lawsuit has now been filed along these lines…

Trump Tariff Saga

Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China last year, apparently believing that imposing higher tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies such as Apple to move their production lines back to the United States.

But of course that was never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to produce consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump insisted that China was paying the tariffs, but the reality is that it is US brands importing finished goods that pay the duties, and the added cost is ultimately passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the height of the saga, tariff rates had soared as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by as much as 25%.

Consumers Should Get Refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose those tariffs unilaterally, and ordered refunds to be paid to US companies — a process that is now under way.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and none of the affected companies has so far indicated any intention of refunding their customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech on this basis, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac Take

The principle is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and are now receiving refunds from the government. Morally, businesses should hand that money back to the consumers who bought their products during that period.

In practice, however, the difficulties are enormous. Logitech would need to identify every transaction made through a vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers paid, and calculate what proportion of those prices was attributable to tariffs.

If this lawsuit succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it is worth bearing in mind that in class actions, it is usually the lawyers who benefit, and the average payout to consumers tends to be quite small.
